Full ablation does not lose answers by cutting them short. On the 32 problems that only ×0.2 solves, ×0 writes answers of the same length (210 against 209 tokens), and only 3 of them are cut off. So ×0 loses through worse reasoning, which confirms that head 3 does useful work at a modest strength. Use of the "####" marker falls as the head is damped (0.32 → 0.26 → 0.20). This does not affect grading here, because the grader falls back to the last number.

The ×0.5 edit is saved (head 3 output block exactly halved, other heads identical) and logged. I now run it paired on the same slice to map the right side of the dose curve.

The dose curve for head 3 on DEV[1024:1250] (original 18.6%) now has a clear peak:

| Head 3 output strength | Paired change |
|---|---|
| ×1 (original) | 0 |
| ×0.5 | +11.5 ± 2.5 (30 wrong→right, 4 right→wrong) |
| ×0.2 | +18.6 ± 3.1 |
| ×0 | +11.1 ± 3.0 |
| spike-only removal | −0.9 |

So head 3's strength itself is the lever. At full strength it holds the model back by about 19 points. At around 0.2 its useful function is kept while the harm is removed, and with the head removed entirely about 8 of those points are lost again.

Whole-head scaling is a coarse fix, though. If the harm is a specific thing head 3 carries — for example a broadcast of the end-of-prompt state it attends to (about 24% of its attention at answer time) — then a rank-1 edit might remove the harm and keep more of the useful function.

Before spending a pass on such a variant (T1), I look it up on summary vectors only. I compute the mean value vector at the last prompt token (V_last), using the same layer-input convention as my earlier run, and the mean value vector over answer tokens. Then I check three things:
- how aligned these two are;
- how large each head's write of V_last is;
- what share of head 3's weights T1 would remove.

T1 itself projects the V_last direction out of head 3's value-side input. If V_last is nearly the same direction as the answer-token mean, T1 is a "remove h3's constant write" edit. If not, it specifically cuts the end-of-prompt broadcast. I find my earlier code first, so the layer indexing is consistent.

That search matched itself (block 153). The earlier computation of each head's output for the mean end-of-prompt state was block 147, so I print its relevant lines. That fixes the layer index and normalisation convention for V_last before I build anything. I also check the shapes of the stored generation activations: residuals at the last prompt token and averaged over answer tokens, from pass 1 of the original model.

My earlier block 147 read the residual at index 10 as the input to L11. In this tool's convention (0 = embeddings, l = after layer l, 27 entries), the input to `model.layers.11` is index 11, so those numbers were one layer early. The conclusions were drawn only from summary statistics and the edits themselves were measured in real passes, so nothing tested is affected, but I use index 11 from now on.

I recompute the mean value vectors at the true L11 input (with the input-norm scale folded in), for the last prompt token (V_last) and for the mean answer state (V_ans). From them I get:
- their norms and how aligned they are;
- each head's write of V_last;
- the share of head 3's weights that T1 would remove.

T1 projects the V_last direction out of head 3's output columns on the value side. It is a rank-1 edit on 256 columns: head 3 then no longer writes the content it retrieves from the end-of-prompt token, but keeps everything else it does.

If T1 matches ×0.2 (about +18), the harm is specifically head 3's broadcast of the end-of-prompt state. If it does little, the harm lies in what head 3 retrieves elsewhere, and whole-head damping remains the edit. I save T1 and log it for the next pass.
